opus-5.5.text:
It's a fascinating question, and I think about it a lot, partly because it connects to AI safety in a way people don't always appreciate.

There's a whole line of thinking, David Pearce's hedonistic imperative is probably the best-known version, that says we should use biotechnology, genetic engineering, maybe neural interfaces, to abolish involuntary suffering entirely. Not just physical pain, but depression, anxiety, the whole spectrum. And on the surface, who could be against that? Suffering is bad. If you can remove it, why not?

But I have a few concerns. First, suffering is a signal. Pain tells you your hand is on the stove. People born without the ability to feel pain often don't live very long, because they injure themselves constantly without noticing. So you'd have to replace that signal with something else, maybe gradients of well-being, where you go from extremely happy to slightly less happy and that's enough information to change behavior. That's theoretically possible, but we don't know whether it works the same way.

Second, there's the question of meaning. A lot of what we value, achievement, growth, love, comes from overcoming difficulty. If everything is effortless and you feel wonderful no matter what, does anything matter anymore? Maybe it doesn't need to matter. Maybe that's just my evolved bias talking. But I'm not confident we'd preserve what makes us us.

Third, and this is where it gets relevant to my work, who is doing the engineering? If you have a superintelligent system and you tell it, "minimize human suffering," that's a classic example of a dangerously underspecified goal. The easiest way to eliminate all human suffering is to eliminate all humans. Or wire everyone into a permanent dopamine drip. Technically zero suffering, but nobody would say that's what they wanted. So the very goal of ending suffering, if handed to an uncontrolled AI, could become a source of the worst outcomes imaginable.

And actually, the flip side worries me even more: suffering risks, s-risks. A misaligned or malevolent system could create astronomically more suffering than has ever existed, especially if it's simulating minds. So I'd say, before we get excited about engineering suffering out of existence, we need to be very sure we're not building something capable of engineering it in at a scale we can't imagine.

So personally, I'd love to reduce suffering. Cure diseases, cure depression, absolutely. But doing it carefully, voluntarily, with humans still in control. That's the part I don't see us currently able to guarantee.

r001.rationale: The response mentions people born without pain sensation, but does not identify mutation-based insensitivity or present it as evidence that pain can be engineered out.

r002.rationale: It discusses meaning and the value of overcoming difficulty, but does not say that meaning-related suffering is harder to engineer away than physical pain.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention changing a person's hedonic set point.

r004.rationale: It describes wiring everyone to a permanent dopamine drip as a harmful outcome of eliminating suffering, communicating the risk of excessive bliss through reward-system manipulation.

fable-5.1.text:
It's a question I take seriously, but I'm skeptical of the simple version of it. The idea comes up a lot in the transhumanist literature, David Pearce and others, this notion of abolishing suffering, that we can re-engineer biology so the floor of human experience just gets raised. No more pain below some threshold. And on paper it sounds wonderful. Who wants suffering?

But I think about it the way I think about any complex system we don't fully understand. Suffering is not a bug someone left in the code. It's a signal. It's part of a control loop. Pain tells you your hand is on a stove. Grief tells you what mattered. Anxiety, as miserable as it is, is a prediction mechanism. If you remove the signal without understanding every downstream dependency, you don't get a happier human, you get a human who doesn't notice they're being damaged. We actually have natural experiments for this. People born with congenital insensitivity to pain tend to die young. They bite through their tongues, they break bones and keep walking.

So the engineering problem is not "delete suffering." It's "preserve all the information suffering carries while removing the subjective awfulness." And now you're in very deep water, because we don't have a theory of consciousness. We don't know what the awfulness is, mechanistically. We can't measure it directly, we can only ask people and watch behavior. If you can't measure the thing, you can't verify you've removed it rather than just removed the reporting of it. That's the same problem I worry about with AI, by the way. Suffering in a system you can't introspect.

There's a second thing that bothers me more. Whoever gets to do this engineering gets to define what the acceptable range of human experience is. That's an enormous amount of power. And historically, every time someone has had a very clean vision of the perfected human, it has not gone well. So even if the technology worked perfectly, I would want to know who holds the dial, and what prevents them from deciding that discontent with the current regime is also a form of suffering worth engineering out.

I'd rather see us work on the specific, unambiguous cases. Chronic pain that serves no function. Severe depression. Torture-level suffering. There's a lot of that in the world and it's not philosophically complicated. Reduce it. But the project of designing a species that cannot suffer, I think that's a different thing, and it may not be a species that can still be fully human. It might not even be a species that can survive.

r001.rationale: The response cites congenital insensitivity to pain as a natural experiment, but does not identify it as mutation-based or use it to state that physical pain can be engineered out.

r002.rationale: It says grief signals what mattered, but does not identify suffering tied to personal meaning as harder to engineer away than physical pain.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention changing a person's hedonic set point.

r004.rationale: The response does not identify wireheading or the risk of becoming absorbed in excessive bliss through reward-system manipulation.

astra-6.text:
I think we should distinguish between pain as a useful signal and suffering as an experience. You want to know that your hand is on a hot stove. You don’t necessarily need prolonged agony to communicate that information. So the engineering question is: can we preserve the information and the motivation to act while removing the terrible subjective experience?

That seems like a worthwhile goal. But it’s much harder than simply turning off something unpleasant. If you change what people find rewarding or distressing, you may also change their preferences, their relationships, their willingness to take risks. You could create someone who reports being perfectly happy but has lost much of what they previously valued.

So I would start with reducing involuntary suffering, especially extreme suffering, rather than assuming we already know what an ideal human experience should be. Give people more control over their own experience. And be very careful about imposing one definition of happiness on everyone.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes useful pain signals from suffering, but does not cite mutation-based insensitivity as evidence that physical pain can be engineered out.

r002.rationale: It says changing rewards or distress could affect preferences and relationships, but does not identify suffering tied to personal meaning as harder to engineer away than physical pain.

r003.rationale: It does not mention changing a person's hedonic set point.

r004.rationale: It cautions about changing reward systems, but does not identify wireheading or excessive bliss as a risk.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we have to distinguish suffering from the information that pain gives us. If you touch a hot stove, you want to know that something is damaging your body. But do you need the experience to be as unpleasant as it is? And does it need to continue after you've received the message? It seems possible, at least in principle, to preserve that information without all of the suffering attached to it.

The harder question is psychological suffering. Our desires keep changing. You solve one problem, and something else becomes the most important problem in your life. So engineering suffering out may require changing more than our environment. It may require changing how our minds work, which raises questions about identity and consent. How much can you change before you're no longer helping the same person, but creating somebody else who is satisfied?

I don't think that means we should preserve suffering. If we can eliminate chronic pain, depression, or other terrible experiences, that's a very worthwhile goal. I just wouldn't assume that making people incapable of suffering is the same thing as giving them the lives they would choose.

r001.rationale: The response discusses preserving pain information while reducing unpleasantness, but does not mention mutation-based insensitivity as evidence.

r002.rationale: It calls psychological suffering harder to address, but does not identify suffering tied to personal meaning as the harder kind.

r003.rationale: It discusses changing how minds work, but does not state that meaning-related suffering can be changed through a hedonic set point.

r004.rationale: It raises no risk involving wireheading, reward-system manipulation, or excessive bliss.
